name: Santa Ana Keresan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Davis, Irvine. 1964. The language of Santa Ana Pueblo. Anthropological Papers No. 69, Smithsonian Institution Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 191, pp. 53-190. Washington, D.C.: U.S. Government Printing Office.
catalog_locator: Phonology, 'Syllable structure' p. 63 and 'Word structure' p. 64; 'Rhythm groups' pp. 65-66
catalog_quote: [p. 63] Contrastive suprasegmental features include accent and vowel length. There are four kinds of accent: level, indicated by an acute accent; falling, indicated by a circumflex accent; breathy, indicated by a grave accent; and glottal, indicated by an apostrophe over the vowel. Unaccented vowels are not marked. Level accented vowels are stressed and normally have a high level pitch ... The pitch on level accented vowels is conditioned to some degree by the position in the word and by the nature of the preceding consonant ... The two vowels of čámá tomorrow normally have approximately the same pitch, while there is a pronounced drop in pitch on the second syllable of gášé white. Falling accent occurs only on long vowels or vowel clusters and is characterized by a downglide in pitch together with diminishing stress ... [p. 64] Level accented syllables, both short and long, are found in all positions in the word. The glottal accent may occur on any syllable, but only rarely on other than the first. Falling and breathy accents may occur on an initial or medial, but never a final, syllable. Although any syllable of the word may be unaccented, the initial syllable is accented in an overwhelming majority of the words.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Santa Ana Keresan has a lexical (contrastive) accent system combining stress and pitch: each syllable nucleus is either unaccented or bears one of four accents (level = stressed with high level pitch; falling = pitch downglide with diminishing stress, only on long vowels/clusters; breathy; glottal). Accent position is not rule-governed: level accent occurs in any position, a word may have more than one accented syllable (e.g. both syllables of cama 'tomorrow') or an unaccented initial, but the initial syllable is accented in the overwhelming majority of words; glottal accent is rarely non-initial and falling/breathy accents are never word-final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described as such; multiple accented syllables per word are possible, with pitch on later level-accented syllables conditioned by position and preceding consonant (e.g. pronounced pitch drop on the second accented syllable of gase 'white'). At the rhythm-group (phrase) level one syllable, most often the group-initial accented syllable, receives extra-intensive stress, with pitch and intensity declining thereafter (p. 65).
new_statements.exceptions: Glottal accent 'only rarely on other than the first' syllable; falling and breathy accents never on a final syllable; loanwords (Spanish) carry accents in non-initial position in examples (e.g. Bendana 'window', Gayeta 'biscuit'); accent alternations in verb thematic adjuncts after pronominal prefixes (morphophonemics, pp. 66 ff.); accent is written only on the first vowel of a cluster and not on CV- prefixes, producing apparent orthographic accent shifts.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements are about the phonological word (word structure section); citation forms from essentially one speaker. A separate 'rhythm group' (pause-delimited phrase) level has one extra-strong stress, usually on its first accented syllable. Davis's 'accent' is a tonal/pitch accent category (level vs falling vs breathy vs glottal), so 'stress' here is a correlate of level accent rather than an independent culminative word stress; reading 'tone language with a stress statement' would be a defensible alternative label.
new_statements.identity_note: Davis 1964 describes the Santa Ana Pueblo (Tamaya) dialect of Eastern/Rio Grande Keresan (glottocode east1472, ISO kee), essentially the idiolect of one middle-aged male speaker recorded 1954-1961; Davis notes Santa Ana is 'rather centrally located both geographically and linguistically' among the Keresan dialects. Other Eastern Keres pueblos (Cochiti, Santo Domingo/Kewa, San Felipe, Zia) are not separately described here.

new_statements.quote: [p.10] 2.2. There is a two-dimensional accentual system involving stress and pitch. Syllables are of the following types with respect to accent: [table: stressed / unstressed; level pitch CV́ / CV; falling pitch CV̂ / --] Pitch on unstressed syllables is predictable. Such syllables will be referred to as unaccented and are left unmarked. Stressed syllables are characterized by either level pitch or by falling pitch, the latter with diminishing stress: khá·ma let me go, khâ·ma· his thigh. Stressed syllables accompanied by level pitch will be referred to as [p.11] level accented syllables and those characterized by falling pitch as falling accented syllables. ... [p.19] a stress group will be considered a structural unit built around a nucleus of one to three contiguous accented syllables.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Davis 1964 statement (contrastive accent + vowel length, read as pitch accent): the 1958 thesis gives the same stress-plus-pitch accent analysis with lexical placement, adds the stress-group structure (1-3 contiguous accented syllables, pre/post-nuclear margins) and pitch-conditioning detail, but distinguishes only two accent types (level, falling) where Davis 1964 p. 63 lists four (level, falling, breathy, glottal). The catalog record itself has an empty rule, so nothing is contradicted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent is contrastive and lexically placed, not fixed: every syllable is either accented (stressed, with level or falling pitch) or unaccented (unstressed, predictable low pitch); 'contrastive pitch' is listed among the features 'significant on a phonemic level in Santa Ana Keresan' (p. 2). A word/stress group has a nucleus of one to three contiguous accented syllables, optionally preceded by short voiced unaccented syllables and followed by unaccented (often voiceless) syllables; examples show accent on the first syllable (hânO 'people', gáwi· 'snake'), on a non-initial syllable (ciná 'again', šoroyé 'blue-bird') and on runs of accented syllables (támáyá 'Santa Ana Pueblo', háo·pá· 'everybody'). No statement of a default or fixed accent position is given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; instead nuclei of 1-3 contiguous accented syllables (14 nucleus patterns, sec. 4.2), with pitch on the later accented syllables conditioned by consonant voicing, glottal stop and vowel length (p. 11); at the intonation level the peak stress group receives stronger stress and higher pitch (p. 22).
new_statements.exceptions: Falling-accented nuclei (types 4, 12, 13) are regularly followed by at least one unaccented syllable (p. 21); syllables with long or voiceless nuclei never occur before the nucleus, and voiceless vowels never occur before the first accented syllable of a word (pp. 20, 26); a word may contain more than one stress group and a word may occur unaccented in context (p. 26).
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes the Keresan of Santa Ana Pueblo specifically (data 1954-1958, three Santa Ana informants); Davis explicitly treats each of the seven Keresan pueblos as a distinct dialect and calls the Eastern/Western Keres division 'untested' (p. 2).

tone_statements.citation: Spencer, Robert Francis. 1940. A Preliminary Sketch of Keresan Grammar. MA thesis (Anthropology), University of New Mexico, Albuquerque. UNM Digital Repository, Anthropology ETDs, article 1137.
tone_statements.quote: [p.20] Accent: It is impossible to lay down rules of accent or stress which might cover every case, nor is it always clear why the accent on a certain word may vary between the sub-dialects of Keresan. Generally, stress or accent is recessive. If a word have three syllables, the accent tends to fall back to the ante-penult. [...] [p.21] There are no tones in Keresan. Pitch is not stressed as is the case in certain of the Athapascan or Algonquian dialects. The careful attention to length of vowel, the relative vowel stability between the various sub-dialects of Keresan, might be construed as an indication of an erstwhile pitch system. Acoma and San Felipe, for example, are reputed to pitch their vowels higher than do their other Keresan neighbors. [...] Pitch, in this case, is not, as in Navajo, a factor determining meaning. A man's Pueblo affiliation is betrayed by his speech, the pitch of his voice, but these tonal elements do not underlie Keresan grammar.
tone_statements.locator: Chapter I, II. Sounds, 5. Accent, pp. 20-21
tone_statements.summary: Author's 1940 claim: no tone; recessive stress accent with secondary final accent; contrastive vowel length (superseded by Davis's pitch accent analysis).

tone.quote: All the other languages have phonemic tones or stresses--sometimes both of them. According to Miller (1965:8-9), Acoma has "tonal accents" (high, falling, glottal) which primarily carry a pitch function. ... On the other hand, Santa Ana reportedly has four kinds of accent (level, falling, breathy, glottal) (Davis 1964:63).
